etymology: Pure ideograph (指事): a single horizontal stroke — one counting rod laid on the ground. The simplest possible written sign, unchanged since oracle-bone script.
mnemonic: One stroke, one finger laid flat, one horizon. Everything in the writing system is built on top of this line — it is the floor the other kanji stand on.

etymology: Ideograph: two counting rods. The upper stroke is slightly shorter, as when two rods are laid neatly one above the other.
mnemonic: Two shelves: a short one on top, a long one below. Count them out loud — に, に — like knocking twice on a door.

etymology: Ideograph: three counting rods. Heaven, humankind and earth in the old Chinese reading of the three lines — top, middle, bottom.
mnemonic: Three floors of a building seen from the side. The middle floor is the smallest — the child between two parents.

etymology: Originally written as four stacked bars (亖); the current form — breath dispersing from a mouth, drawn as legs inside a box — was borrowed for its sound over 2,000 years ago.
mnemonic: A window (the box) with a pair of legs dangling out of it: four legs in all if you count the window's own two sides. よん — the yawn of someone climbing out of that window.

etymology: Ideograph: originally an X between two horizontal lines — a tally device marking the halfway point of ten. The X 'crosses over' at five.
mnemonic: The tally-keeper's shortcut: when you reach five, you stop drawing sticks and cross them off — ご! Four strokes that mean one full hand of fingers.

etymology: Originally the pictograph of a small hut with a roof; the word for 'six' was written with it purely for its sound (rebus borrowing).
mnemonic: A tiny hut: pointed roof on top, two legs for walls. Six people are crammed inside — ろく, they groan, as the roof creaks.

etymology: Originally a picture of a line being cut crosswise — it was the first way of writing 切 'to cut'. Borrowed early on for the number seven.
mnemonic: An upside-down seven with a hook. A knife slicing diagonally through a line: cut a cake into seven pieces — しち slices.

etymology: Ideograph: two strokes leaning away from each other — the act of dividing something in two. Eight is the number you reach by halving three times (2·2·2).
mnemonic: Two ski tracks parting on the slope. Divide, divide, divide: 2, 4, 8 — はち. The strokes never touch, like a pie split for sharing.

etymology: Originally a pictograph of a bent elbow with a hand reaching in — borrowed for the number nine since oracle-bone times.
mnemonic: A baseball pitcher's arm frozen mid-throw, elbow bent, wrist hooked: nine innings, きゅう. The hook at the end is the ball leaving the hand.

etymology: Originally a single vertical stroke (a needle — the ancestor of 針); a dot, later a crossbar, was added to distinguish it. Borrowed for 'ten': one full crossing of both hands' fingers.
mnemonic: A perfect cross: all ten fingers of two open hands meeting at right angles. じゅう — the intersection where the count is complete.

etymology: Pictograph (象形): an open mouth, squared off by the brush. One of the most productive components in the writing system — anything spoken, eaten or shouted tends to contain it.
mnemonic: A wide-open mouth turned into a square frame. Every time you spot this box in a kanji, someone is talking, eating or shouting — くち.

etymology: Pictograph: the sun — originally a circle with a dot at its center, squared by the brush into a rectangle with a bar. One sun crossing the sky = one day.
mnemonic: A window with the blind half-drawn: through it, the sun. One sunrise per day — ひ, the sun; にち, the day it makes.

etymology: Pictograph: the crescent moon with two shading strokes inside. One full cycle of the moon = one month.
mnemonic: The sun's window (日) grew legs and slimmed down for the night shift: the moon. It waxes and wanes once a month — つき / ゲツ, as in 月曜日, the moon's own day.

etymology: Pictograph: an eye with its pupil, drawn horizontally on the oracle bones and later stood upright by the brush.
mnemonic: An eye standing on end: the two inner bars are the iris and pupil. Stack it next to 日 and 月 — sun, moon, and the め that watches them both.

etymology: Compound ideograph (会意) by the classic account: ten (十) mouths (口) — a story that has passed through ten generations of tellers is old indeed.
mnemonic: Ten mouths have told this tale before yours: it is ancient — ふるい. Picture a weathered cross planted over a stone box, standing there for centuries.

etymology: Origin debated: commonly explained as a ray of light breaking from the sun (日 with a spark on top), or as a white acorn. Its 'bright, plain' sense is ancient.
mnemonic: The first drop of daylight hitting the sun's window at dawn: everything bleaches white — しろ. A sunbeam with the brightness turned all the way up.

etymology: Phono-semantic (形声): one (一) on top for the count, white (白) beneath lending the ancient sound. One 'white' = one hundred.
mnemonic: One (一) white (白) hair — the first of a hundred to come, says your grandmother. ひゃく! Count to one hundred and you've earned exactly one white hair.

etymology: Ideograph: a pole planted through the exact center of a camp or banner — dead middle. Oracle-bone forms show a flagpole with streamers.
mnemonic: An arrow through the bullseye of a target box: right in the middle — なか. In compounds it means 'inside' or 'throughout': 中国, the Middle Country.

etymology: Formed in oracle-bone script from person (人) + one (一) as a phonetic-numeric device: 'one (unit of) persons' = a thousand.
mnemonic: A ten (十) wearing a swept hat: promoted a hundred ranks overnight — せん, one thousand. The hat is the zero-multiplier.

etymology: Pure ideograph: a short mark placed above a base line. Its twin 下 puts the mark below. Among the oldest abstract signs in the script.
mnemonic: A little flag planted on top of the ground line: up, above — うえ. The vertical stroke grows upward like a sapling; nothing hangs below the line.

etymology: Pure ideograph: a short mark placed under a base line — the mirror of 上. The pair appears together on the oldest oracle bones.
mnemonic: A root and a drop hanging under the ground line: down, below — した. Flip 上 in a mirror along the ground and it falls to become 下.

etymology: Compound ideograph: an eye (目) set on human legs (儿) — a person shown as nothing but their looking. To see is to walk your eye over to something.
mnemonic: An eyeball that grew legs and runs around looking at things — みる. When you 'go see' a friend, this little creature is what you send ahead.

etymology: Simplification of 萬, originally the pictograph of a scorpion, borrowed since antiquity for the number 10,000.
mnemonic: A scorpion with its tail curled — count its swarm of eggs: ten thousand, まん. In prices it swings that tail through your wallet: 一万円.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a left hand (𠂇) holding a carpenter's tool (工). The left hand steadies the work while the right one acts.
mnemonic: The hand that holds the ruler (工) while the other draws: your left — ひだり. Stroke tip: here the horizontal goes first, then the sweep — the mirror of 右.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a hand (𠂇) over a mouth (口) — the right hand, the one you eat with and raise to speak or swear.
mnemonic: The hand that carries food to the mouth: your right — みぎ. Stroke tip: the sweep goes first here, then the horizontal — mirror etiquette to 左.

etymology: Pictograph: a swaddled baby — big head, arms spread wide, legs bound together in the wrapping cloth.
mnemonic: A baby with arms flung out and its legs still wrapped in a blanket — こ. Girls' names end with it (花子), and it hides in 好き: a woman with her child, fondness itself.

etymology: Pictograph: a figure kneeling with hands crossed — the posture of a woman in ancient formal dress. The three strokes still trace the crossed arms and folded legs.
mnemonic: A dancer mid-curtsy, arms crossing her body — おんな. In compounds she signals the feminine: 女の子, girl; 彼女, she.

etymology: Pictograph: the woman sign (女) with two dots added for the breasts — a nursing mother. One of the most transparent kanji in the script.
mnemonic: A woman with two dots: the mother who nursed you — はは. The frame around the dots is her embrace; every stroke leans inward, protective.

etymology: Ideograph: three tiny points — grains of sand or slivers falling away from a blade. Smallness shown by sheer lack of material.
mnemonic: A hook with two shy drops hiding on either side: something so small it barely exists — ちいさい. The vertical stroke is a needle; the drops, its parings.

etymology: Derived from 小 (small) with an extra stroke shaving something off — smaller still in quantity: few, scarce.
mnemonic: Take 'small' (小) and slice one more piece off with a diagonal cut: now there's hardly any left — すこし, すくない.

etymology: Pictograph: a person standing with arms and legs stretched wide — the human body making itself as big as it can.
mnemonic: 'How big was the fish?' — arms flung wide: THIS big! おおきい. A stick figure showing off maximum size with its whole body.

etymology: Compound ideograph: two evenings (夕) stacked — night after night after night. Repetition itself made visible: many.
mnemonic: Two crescent moons piled up like plates after a feast: one evening wasn't enough, there were many — おおい. Stack anything twice in kanji and it multiplies.

etymology: Compound ideograph: evening (夕) + divination crack (卜). Divination performed at evening, outside the proper morning ritual — hence 'outside, other'.
mnemonic: At dusk (夕) the fortune-teller reads cracks (卜) in a bone by the city gate — outside the walls, where the wild things are: そと, 外国 the lands outside.

etymology: Compound ideograph: evening (夕) + mouth (口). In the dark you cannot be seen — so you call out your name to be known.
mnemonic: Too dark to see faces at dusk, so a mouth calls into the night: 'It's me!' — your name, なまえ. The password that works when eyes don't.

etymology: Pictograph: three lines of flowing water between two banks — a river drawn exactly as it looks from a hill.
mnemonic: Three currents running side by side downhill — かわ. The outer strokes are the banks, the middle one the fast water. Found in half the place-names of Japan (小川, 川口).

etymology: Pictograph: a central current with droplets splashing to both sides. As a left-side component it compresses into the three drops of 氵.
mnemonic: A river seen head-on: the main stream down the middle, spray flying left and right — みず. Its on-reading スイ flows through 水曜日, Wednesday, the water day.

etymology: Pictograph: a mound of earth raised on the ground line — the altar of the soil god in its oldest form.
mnemonic: A little pile of dirt on the ground with a sprout's cross planted in it — つち. Saturday, 土曜日, is the day you dig in the garden.

etymology: Phono-semantic: sun (日) gives the meaning — time measured by the sun — while 寺 (temple) lends the reading ジ. Temples were the timekeepers, ringing the hours.
mnemonic: The temple bell tolls as the sun moves: that is how you know the hour — とき, ジ. 何時ですか — 'what time is it?' asks the sun of the temple.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a woman (女) at rest under a roof (宀) — peace, safety, ease. 'Cheap' grew later from 'easy on the purse'.
mnemonic: Home at last, under her own roof, she finally relaxes — やすい. And relax your wallet too: this shop is 安い, reassuringly cheap.

etymology: Pictograph: a tree — trunk, spreading branches, roots below. Doubled it becomes a wood (林), tripled a forest (森).
mnemonic: Trunk up the middle, branches out, roots down — き. Thursday, 木曜日, is the tree's day. Wherever wood is worked, this kanji stands at the left of the character.

etymology: Ideograph: a tree (木) with a stroke marking its base — the root, the origin. Books came later: the 'root' of knowledge, and paper from the tree itself.
mnemonic: Mark the root of the tree: that is where everything begins — もと. From that root comes paper, and from paper the ほん you're reading. 日本: the land at the sun's root.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a foot (止, worn to a slanted form) above walking legs (儿) — a footprint out in front of the walker: whoever went ahead, before.
mnemonic: Fresh footprints ahead of you on the trail: someone went before — さき. The 先生 is simply the one 'born before' you, walking the path first.

etymology: By the classic account: nuggets (the two dots) buried in layered earth (土) under a cover (𠆢) — metal in the mine. Later 'metal' in general, then gold and money.
mnemonic: Under a little roof, in the earth, two nuggets gleam — かね, gold, money. Friday, 金曜日, is payday: the day the nuggets reach your pocket.

etymology: Compound ideograph: movement (辶) + head (首) — walking with your head leading you: the road you follow, and figuratively the Way (as in 柔道, 茶道).
mnemonic: Your head out in front, feet rolling beneath it down the path — みち. Every martial art ends in this kanji: the road you walk your whole life, ドウ.

etymology: Pictograph: a cart seen from above — the axle running vertically, the wheel-body in the middle, crossbars at each end.
mnemonic: Bird's-eye view of a chariot: axle, cabin, two wheels — くるま. Two millennia later it still parks inside 電車 and 自転車 without a scratch.

etymology: Originally a foot aboard a boat gliding forward — 'to advance'; the blade (刂) entered the character early as a graphic-phonetic addition. 'In front, before' is the settled meaning.
mnemonic: On the prow of the boat, blade in hand, cutting the water ahead: everything in front of you — まえ. 名前 puts your name out front for the world.

etymology: Pictograph: a flame rising from a burning pile, sparks flying off both sides. As a bottom component it flattens into four dots (灬).
mnemonic: A campfire: the central blaze and two sparks leaping away — ひ. Tuesday, 火曜日, is fire's day. Keep it away from 木 unless you want ashes.

etymology: Phono-semantic: the grass crown (艹) gives the meaning — a plant — while 化 'change, transform' lends the reading カ. The plant transformed into its loveliest state: a flower.
mnemonic: Under the grass crown, a plant works its transformation (化) — and blooms: はな. 花見 is the festival of watching that magic happen.

etymology: Pictograph: a whole fish — head at the top (𠂊), scaled body (田), and a tail that later flattened into four dots (灬).
mnemonic: Head, scaly belly, flick of a tail: a fish drawn head-up as if hauled from the water — さかな. The four dots are drops still falling from its fins.
